title: Agentic workflows: Tacit expertise resists easy transfer
desc: Combines tools, client context and expert testing while recognizing open-ended legal quality and retained human checkpoints.

kps.k: The central proposition is that legal AI gains practical value by combining model capabilities with expert-designed workflows, tools and client context.
kps.d: The debate moves beyond whether models can generate legal text to whether organisations can turn that capability into dependable work. Harvey’s Winston Weinberg identifies process data, evaluation and workflow design as major constraints; Orbital’s Andrew Thompson argues that practice-specific knowledge and tools must close gaps that prompting alone cannot. This complements, rather than negates, the argument that law’s text-heavy, precedent-based work suits language models. The supporting material mainly comprises development experience and conceptual reasoning, not independently validated comparisons.

qs.q: Because I think the reasoning ability of these models is is is there actually I think the bigger problem is like evaluation, improving process um and collecting more data too.
qs.a: Winston Weinberg (Harvey) — Sequoia Training Data Ep.33 · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: It requires not just prompting the model better, it requires sort of proprietary knowledge or some of the tools that you’re giving it.
qs.a: Orbital CTO Andrew Thompson on Practice Area AI, Real Estate Law, and the Future of Legal Work · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

kps.k: Agentic development shifts the unit of automation from an isolated answer to a connected sequence of work, without necessarily removing human checkpoints.
kps.d: Harvey describes reusable research and extraction components coordinated across workflows. The Arredondo–Hron discussion describes research agents planning, using KeyCite and replanning after dead ends; Norm describes background first-pass analysis with persistent client context. Current reported deployments include Crosby’s routing agent and LegalOn’s intake agent. These narrower implementations do not establish autonomous completion of complex matters. The source predicting end-to-end legal work in 2026 retains human oversight, while Nick Fleisher regards entirely unsupervised in-house workflows as distant or potentially unattainable. Niki Black also warns that disputed definitions obscure what users actually delegate.

qs.q: results and what we see with deep research I think is really like I said a profound shift in these models being able to certainly write good plans in the same way a legal researcher would write these plans but also to be able to leverage these tools like KeyCite or the Key Number system to go follow a bunch of breadcrumb trails and see where they lead and if they lead to dead ends back up and and replan.
qs.a: Pablo Arredondo and Joel Hron on Reasoning Models, Deep Research, and the Future of Legal AI · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

qs.q: Today we've basically built a parallegal agent and which is like in charge of routing all the work from like you know  that comes in from our like customers in the same way that a parallegal would at a law firm and then routes it to a human lawyer and make sure the work is assigned effectively.
qs.a: Ryan Daniels & John Sarihan (Crosby) — Sequoia Training Data Ep.61 · AI-native providers · 2026

kps.k: Tacit expertise and client-specific judgment are both proposed training assets and difficult knowledge-transfer problems.
kps.d: Pereyra argues that public final documents omit the partner corrections and decisions needed to improve models. Nay proposes continuously maintained client overlays, while Crosby stresses playbooks, business knowledge and negotiation history. Daniels’ account of being unable to explain some of his own contract-review decisions qualifies the assumption that expertise can simply be recorded and transferred. Reed and Summize’s Tom Dunlop add that useful context requires curated documents, metadata and company-specific priorities, not merely larger uploads. Confidentiality, ethical walls and permissions constrain access to these assets.

qs.q: But I think the really big opportunity for law firms is how do they take all of the internal partner feedback and data that they've created and use that to start training.
qs.a: Gabe Pereyra — Harvey (No Priors Ep. 142) · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

qs.q: And and that that's one thing and then the second thing is around uh how do you have a process and  a technology to tailor that base AI agent to a given client's context and then work super closely with the client to keep that updated and and have that be sort of a living breathing AI agent that understands uh the specifics and the nuances of of their firm.
qs.a: John Nay — Norm Ai / Norm Law (founder interview) · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

kps.k: Legal quality often lacks a single correct answer, complicating evaluation and the transfer of coding-style reinforcement learning.
kps.d: Pereyra distinguishes checkable clause extraction from merger drafting that resists binary grading. Scott Stevenson and the Dhein discussion emphasise legitimate disagreement among competent lawyers; Crosby proposes alignment to an individual lawyer, assuming internal consistency. John Rizner reports research in which model families gave different breach-of-contract recommendations, but supplies no numerical findings or detailed methods here. These arguments distinguish factual or linguistic error from defensible differences in risk appetite, negotiation strategy and jurisprudence. Schwarcz nevertheless expects capability gains while acknowledging law’s weaker feedback loops.

qs.q: But for something like generate this merger agreement,  >> it's really hard to just give some  binary like this is good or this is bad.
qs.a: Gabe Pereyra — Harvey (No Priors Ep. 142) · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

qs.q: It's not necessary saying that either of those lawyers is wrong or one model is better than the other.
qs.a: E38 - How Will SaaSpocalypse Affect AI For Legal: Spellbook CEO Scott Stevenson · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

kps.k: Realistic, expert-reviewed tests offer a route beyond generic benchmarks, but the supplied evidence does not establish broad legal reliability.
kps.d: Harvey describes synthetic data rooms with planted defects, lawyer-written rubrics and its Legal Agent Benchmark spanning 24 practice areas. These methods aim to test realistic work despite restrictions on sharing client data; their descriptions provide no performance scores or validation of transfer to live matters. LegalOn reports double-digit improvements on its own contract benchmark, while Weinberg recounts attorney approval of 86 out of 100 early landlord–tenant answers. Both are bounded company-reported results, not general accuracy measures. Illustrative completion percentages and predictions of future benchmark scores should likewise remain separate from measured findings.

qs.q: We basically mapped out 24 practice  areas that law firms have on their websites, that they have lawyers, associates kind of assigned to within the firm.
qs.a: Gabe Pereyra — Harvey: the legal agent benchmark and the coming token-pricing reckoning · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: We'd see, you know, double digit percentage improvements in our contractory benchmark, which is a set, like a very robust set of tasks that we evaluate foundational models against.
qs.a: Ep 301: From Law Student Startup Founder to Global CEO: Daniel Lewis's Legal Tech Journey · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

kps.k: Human verification supplies accountability, but its cost can limit the value of faster generation.
kps.d: Pereyra argues that source-linked workflows, visible explanations and training in characteristic model errors make review more effective. Shaver insists that reviewers check reasoning, intended meaning and word choice, not citations alone. Leonard asks whether reading an entire case to verify a summary erases the benefit; Marwaha argues that experienced lawyers may sometimes work faster without AI, and Buckley identifies a shift toward expensive quality-assurance work. Fleisher recommends approval controls proportionate to the risk of external actions. Crosby’s reported malpractice coverage and acceptance of liability distinguish accountable service delivery from selling software, without proving that its outputs are error-free.

qs.q: Now when you get a mistake, it’s not just, “Oh, it generated a bunch of text and I don’t know what happened.”  You can say, “Here is the reasoning trace.”  You can see, “Oh, it pulled the wrong case,” or “It summarized the case incorrectly.” Now you understand why it came to the wrong conclusion.
qs.a: When Will Lawyers Trust AI? — Gabe Pereyra (Harvey) · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: When we use AI, even when you try really hard to apply your human judgment, you're you're verifying, but you may not necessarily be thinking, how can I abbreviate this or is this actually saying what I wanted it to say?
qs.a: Nikki Shaver — Legaltech Hub (agentic governance and the efficacy turn) · Market & press · 2026

kps.k: The value of specialist legal applications remains contested, as do the best technical routes to specialisation.
kps.d: LegalOn, GC AI, Orbital and Preston Clark locate differentiation in trustworthy content, precise outputs, verification interfaces and configured workflows. Legora describes orchestration without fine-tuning in one account, whereas Harvey advocates task-specific post-training. LexisNexis and Ironclad favour task-dependent model selection; Junestrand also argues for concentrating engineering around a chosen model. Against claims that specialist products are necessary, AJ Shankar expects general-purpose tools to gain ground in simple transactions, and Dan Mishin considers them adequate for much legal work. These positions concern different tasks and product scopes; the material supplies no common comparative test that resolves them.

qs.q: Yeah, and we've also, we took fundamentally different approaches at the start, where we haven't done any fine tuning of the models.
qs.a: Leya Rebrands as Legora: Collaborative AI for Lawyers · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

qs.q: But the best way to do fine tuning in post training is task specific.
qs.a: How AI Breakout Harvey is Transforming Legal Services, with CEO Winston Weinberg · Market & press · 2025

kps.k: Implementation requires organisational investment and workflow redesign, not merely purchasing or quickly building an AI interface.
kps.d: Skoghag recommends starting with the underlying problem rather than a predetermined AI solution. Legora and Norm describe legal engineers working with practitioners and software engineers; Reed stresses continuing maintenance and monitoring. Abramowitz sees lawyer-built applications as a response to bespoke needs, but this does not eliminate production, security or staffing obligations. The practical choice spans buying, configuring and building, with no universal prescription. Accounts of firm-wide process mapping and AAA’s planned case-management redesign also distinguish replicating existing steps from reconsidering which steps are needed.

qs.q: So for example, how to build an AI enabled workflow, but rather you start off with the core issue.
qs.a: Emelie Skoghag: How Legal Technologists Transform Law Firms · Market & press · 2026

qs.q: All three are collaborating — especially the legal engineer and the partner — every single day to embed that knowledge that the partners have from decades of experience into these AI agents.
qs.a: John Nay — Norm Ai / Norm Law (agentic law and the AI-native full-service firm) · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

kps.k: Commercial and workforce implications depend on task-level outcomes, not on equating automation with whole-role replacement.
kps.d: In-house accounts provide concrete but unvalidated operational claims: Moderna reports contract-specific GPTs answering 90% of business questions, DHL claims 80% time savings in recurring drafting, and Salesforce reports roughly 100-fold speed gains on some tasks. Crosby recommends measuring turnaround, service levels and human touch points, while warning that paying demand does not establish repeatable automation. Harvey seeks to improve loss-leading work through software and flat fees; AI-native providers redesign delivery around first-pass AI. Fleisher rejects current like-for-like staff substitution. The evidence therefore supports examining specific workflows and retained human work rather than inferring department-wide savings or employment effects.

qs.q: But we really are sometimes getting like 100X, faster speed and higher accuracy.
qs.a: The AI Pilot is Over: Legal's Moment to Move Beyond Experiments and Avoid the Innovator's Dilemma (Sabastian Niles, President & CLO Salesforce) · In-house counsel · 2026

qs.q: We need to make sure we're meeting things like our SLA, which is measured by our turnaround time, how many human touch points were involved in actually every contract from start to finish.
qs.a: Ryan Daniels & John Sarihan (Crosby) — Sequoia Training Data Ep.61 · AI-native providers · 2026

kps.k: Expertise may shift toward supervising systems and strategic advice, but how to develop that expertise remains unresolved.
kps.d: Hron proposes that professionals increasingly design tests, guidance and governance around AI execution. Pereyra sees firm knowledge and simulated matters as resources for both agent training and faster associate learning; these remain educational proposals rather than demonstrated outcomes. Schwarcz recommends developing foundational lawyering skills before introducing AI training in later law-school years, while the Supio practitioner warns of junior dependence. Nor does the discussion support a clean division between routine machine work and exclusively human strategy: Pereyra and litigation practitioners also describe AI-assisted brainstorming and strategic preparation. The open question is how to preserve independent judgment while changing the work through which lawyers acquire it.

qs.q: As AI sort of picks up more and more of this grunt work, if you will, your job is more about how do you build systems around AI to do the work you want it to do in the way you want it done, rather than doing the work itself, right?
qs.a: Legal AI, Trust, and Agents: Joel Hron on Thomson Reuters, Anthropic, and the Future of CoCounsel · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: You could say, “I want to run a simulated fund formation, a simulated litigation, a simulated merger,” and go through the process end to end, getting feedback from a simulated client and simulated partners.
qs.a: Harvey's Gabe Pereyra on the Future of Legal AI · Regulators & courts · 2026

vlens.an:
The curated AI-native legal-provider sources accept the principal proposition and materially develop it into an operating model for legal-service delivery. Across Crosby, Norm Law, Covenant, Lawhive and General Legal, practical value is attributed not to model output alone but to integrated workflows, task-specific tools, accessible client and negotiation context, close lawyer–engineer collaboration, expert testing and retained lawyer checkpoints. Several sources add concrete accountability mechanisms: lawyer verification, risk-based escalation, licensed-attorney supervision, regulatory compliance and, at Crosby, provider liability and malpractice coverage.

Their common reasoning is that legal work contains context and judgment that generic prompting cannot reliably reproduce. Experienced lawyers contribute client risk preferences, playbooks, market norms, negotiation history and tacit pattern recognition; engineers must turn those inputs into usable workflow components. AI-native delivery is therefore framed as organisational redesign rather than simply adding a copilot: first-pass analysis, routing, drafting, communications and sometimes back-office processes are connected inside a service operation that can observe and refine how work is performed.

Material variation concerns how far and where automation can proceed. Crosby proposes eventual substitution of tasks associated with increasingly senior lawyers and simulated negotiation, but distinguishes those ambitions from its current routing automation and preserves lawyers for judgment-dependent issues. Berrent predicts lawyer-free delivery for low-end commercial contracts, while Walker and Proner maintain broad attorney oversight, and Mishin expects little AI leverage in some high-stakes deals. The sources also differ on technical specialisation: Crosby emphasises task-specific context, benchmarking and tuning, whereas Mishin considers general-purpose foundation models adequate for much legal work. These differences qualify the scope and route to automation rather than rejecting the proposition.

The evidential basis remains limited. Most support comes from founders’ operating descriptions, practitioner impressions, anecdotes and forecasts. Reported throughput or accuracy claims generally lack disclosed measurement protocols or independent validation, and the sources do not establish dependable autonomous completion of complex legal matters. Their strongest collective contribution is therefore a concrete design and accountability framework for agentic legal services, not proof of broad legal reliability or wholesale role replacement.

qs.q: But to get an LM all the context from all the edge cases that a lawyer seen throughout their career is actually quite difficult.
qs.a: Ryan Daniels — Crosby (AI-native law firm) · AI-native providers · 2025

qs.q: And you can maintain a level of human supervision and oversight over those the work of those AI agents because of course we're in a regulated environment and we ourselves are a regulated firm, a global AI native regulated law firm.
qs.a: Pierre Proner — Lawhive (co-founder) on the $60M Series B and US expansion · AI-native providers · 2026

vlens.an: The selected academia and research sources accept the proposition that dependable legal AI requires more than general model capability and materially develop it in complementary directions. Scott supplies the clearest workflow contribution: legal tasks differ in structure, so tools and methods should be task-specific, with verification built into case-based LLM use and practice-specific models proposed for encoding accumulated expertise. Schwarcz strengthens the human-expertise and evaluation dimensions by arguing that foundational lawyering skills should precede AI training and that law often lacks tight, verifiable feedback loops; he nevertheless predicts substantial future capability gains. Hoffman extends the account of open-ended legal quality through contract interpretation, where competent lawyers can advance competing plausible meanings, and frames models as potentially supplying a majoritarian reading rather than a uniquely correct answer. Material variation therefore concerns emphasis and evidentiary status: Scott focuses on system design and checked outputs, Schwarcz on education and continual empirical reassessment, and Hoffman on a bounded interpretive research hypothesis. Several claims—especially bespoke-model benefits, future capability jumps and improved judicial interpretation—remain proposals or predictions rather than demonstrated performance findings. This characterises only the curated sources supplied, not academia or research generally.

qs.q: And I think having one tool for all kind of legal reasoning doesn't make sense because all legal reasoning is not the same thing.
qs.a: Law as Code & the AI Power Shift · Academia · 2026

qs.q: Reinforcement learning is harder in law because there are not as many verifiable, tight feedback loops you can have.
qs.a: Can AI Make Lawyers Better? — Daniel Schwarcz · Academia · 2026

vlens.an: These curated traditional-law-firm sources accept the proposition that legal AI becomes useful through task-specific, context-rich workflows with retained lawyer judgment, and they add concrete practice-level detail. Nuara develops a risk-tiered model: routine extraction and standard documents can use lightweight lawyer verification, whereas master-agreement drafting requires much more source material and intensive quality review. Devlin-Brown extends the proposition to litigation by proposing persistently case-aware agents rather than repeated, isolated document uploads. Dhein similarly grounds tool selection in task decomposition and stresses that advice depends on client objectives and risk appetite, while the build-or-buy discussion adds the organisational constraint that internal development requires resources and confidence in returns. Material variation concerns maturity and emphasis, not the core proposition: Nuara and Dhein focus on present supervised uses and capability limits; Devlin-Brown anticipates greater future value from case-aware agents but acknowledges that adoption remains basic; and the specialist-product discussion is chiefly a forecast rather than reliability evidence. Collectively, the sources do not establish autonomous performance, broad reliability or easy transfer of tacit expertise.

qs.q: And if you can extract the to and the from and the section of the agreement and so on and so forth, which then can be eyeballed by a partner or an associate, that they’re correct and they can go out, that’s great use of the tool.
qs.a: Flatiron Law Group's Lennie Nuara on Talent-First AI, M&A Workflows, and the Future of Legal Practice · Law firms · 2026

qs.q: Really getting an agent into a case that knows the case.
qs.a: E56 - AI-Pilled, Not AI-First: Arlo Devlin-Brown, Founding Principal, TDB Law · Law firms · 2026

vlens.an: The curated legal-tech vendor sources collectively accept the proposition and materially develop it through concrete implementation models. They describe domain experts encoding process steps, agentic orchestration across tools, firm- and client-specific data layers, curated legal content, task-specific model selection, realistic synthetic matters, expert rubrics, and interfaces for human verification. Common reasoning is that foundation models may supply useful language and reasoning capabilities, but dependable legal work requires substantial application engineering, workflow redesign, authoritative content and professional judgment around them. Material variation concerns the technical route: some favour task-specific fine-tuning, others orchestration without fine-tuning or multi-model selection; some project end-to-end agentic execution with oversight, while others restrict near-term value to bounded tasks or warn that verification costs can erase productivity gains. A few sources discuss only model-level advances or general research benefits, leaving their position unclear. Claims of speed, accuracy and adoption are mostly vendor-reported, anecdotal or prospective, so this alignment should not be read as independent proof of broad reliability or as representative of all legal-tech vendors.

qs.q: And then we also need to be focused on  how do you build the user experiences again to optimize this generation verification loop so that users can build trust very quickly in what they’re doing and what they’re sort of sending off to the judge, right?
qs.a: Pablo Arredondo and Joel Hron on Reasoning Models, Deep Research, and the Future of Legal AI · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

vlens.an: Across this curated set of market-analyst, consultancy and press sources, the professional voice accepts the proposition that dependable legal AI requires more than generic model capability and materially develops it with implementation detail. The clearest extension is Weinberg’s account of combining domain-expert-authored process steps with retrieval, chained models, orchestration and task-specific fine-tuning. Other sources reinforce narrower parts of the proposition: Shaver calls for human verification of reasoning rather than citations alone; Black highlights contested definitions and governance risks around agentic delegation; Skoghag advocates problem-first workflow redesign; Abramowitz argues for workflow-specific lawyer-built applications; and Amsellem and the AI-first-firm discussion stress buyer needs, playbooks, connected data and lawyer involvement. Material variation concerns how specialisation should be delivered—through lawyer-built applications, purchased legal-specific products, or expert-configured platforms—and how far autonomy should extend. The sources also differ in emphasis: some focus on governance and retained checkpoints, while others focus on product architecture, investment opportunity or provider evolution. Their support is predominantly strategic, experiential and anecdotal rather than based on independent comparative testing, and several do not address the synthesis’s harder questions about transferring tacit expertise or evaluating open-ended legal quality.

qs.q: And so what we do is we actually hire domain experts who sit down and say, “These are the steps that I would take,” right?
qs.a: How AI Breakout Harvey is Transforming Legal Services, with CEO Winston Weinberg · Market & press · 2025

vlens.an: This curated set of regulators, courts and professional-body voices broadly accepts the proposition that useful legal AI depends on contextualised workflows, expert input and retained human accountability, and it materially develops that proposition through institutional implementation mechanisms. Common reasons include the need to move beyond isolated text generation, combine legal and technical expertise, redesign whole processes, and constrain AI according to the risk and boundedness of the task. Concrete additions include AAA’s end-to-end workflow mapping before construction, risk-proportionate approval for external actions, legal-first enterprise deployment to identify safe lanes, and task-specific regulatory guardrails such as preventing a system from generating case law. Internal variation is substantial: some sources focus on operational redesign or governance, while others chiefly offer conceptual arguments about law’s language-based character, hypothetical productivity gains, or AI-assisted creativity. The latter provide limited evidence on tacit-knowledge transfer, evaluation or dependable implementation. Views also differ in emphasis rather than direction: Fleisher treats fully autonomous in-house workflows as distant or potentially unattainable, whereas other speakers anticipate disruption to junior work or eventual broader automation but leave supervision questions unresolved. Across the material, claimed benefits are predominantly forecasts, examples and practitioner observations rather than measured demonstrations of broad legal reliability; one source is therefore only loosely connected to the proposition.

qs.q: And that's been a lot of uh workshops and discussions with the business, 20, 30 people in the room, where we're stepping through from intake all the way to award and trying to map that out because then the next step will be to build it.
qs.a: An AI Arbitrator? The Latest Innovations from the American Arbitration Association, with CEO Bridget McCormack and CTO Diana Didia · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: And one of the guardrails I loved was: it can’t generate case law.
qs.a: The UK Just Approved an AI-Only Law Firm. Is the U.S. Ready? — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2025

vlens.an: These selected in-house counsel and legal-operations sources collectively support the proposition that legal AI creates practical value when embedded in bounded, organisation-specific workflows rather than treated as autonomous general-purpose legal capability. Their common reasoning is operational: DHL applies historical in-house work product to recurring drafting; Moderna grounds self-service in individual contracts; Salesforce puts agents in service of client priorities, intake and outside-counsel processes; and the Meta discussion anticipates LLMs becoming integral to business processes. They generally frame automation at task level, with lawyers redirected toward complex work rather than wholly replaced. Material variation concerns maturity and safeguards. DHL describes a concrete workflow with attorney verification, while Moderna combines a reported deployment with predicted contract and e-discovery agents; Salesforce reports qualified task-level gains but acknowledges measurement limitations; and Meta's process integration is mainly prospective. The Ford source supports only the narrower claim that generative AI has improved legal technology's commercial viability and does not address workflow design, client context or human checkpoints. Across the selected sources, performance figures are company-reported and unvalidated, and most do not materially engage with the synthesis's harder questions about tacit-expertise transfer, legal-quality evaluation or the cost of verification. Thus the professional voice supports the principal proposition without independently establishing broad reliability or autonomous completion of complex legal work.

qs.q: I think we will be able to use LLMs to be an integral part of those processes to make them less manual, more efficient.
qs.a: Inside Counsel at Scale · In-house counsel · 2026

elens.an: The 2023–2024 sources support the proposition chiefly by showing that generative AI’s legal value was emerging through bounded applications and task-specific technical choices, rather than through autonomous handling of open-ended legal matters. Common reasons include law’s text-heavy and relatively standardised materials, the sharp reduction in data and development time claimed for contract extraction, and the need to select different models and reliability thresholds for different tasks. Material variation remains: the legal-language and Ford discussions make broad conceptual or commercial-potential claims without addressing expert workflow design, tacit knowledge transfer, evaluation or human checkpoints; Ironclad offers more concrete company-reported development experience and a multi-model strategy, but no independent comparative validation. The period therefore supports the proposition’s practical, workflow-level orientation while providing limited evidence on its harder claims about transferring expert judgment and preserving dependable human oversight.

qs.q: With the help of OpenAI, we are shipping a release this week that adds 179 new fields, which Ironclad can recognize instantly.
qs.a: Assisting Knowledge Workers · Legal-tech vendor · 2023

elens.an:
The curated 2025 sources collectively build on the proposition rather than merely endorsing it. They supply concrete implementation models for turning model capability into legal work: reusable workflow components, agent planning and tool use, curated legal and client data, practice-specific playbooks, process mapping, lawyer–engineer collaboration, expert evaluation, dedicated validation software and risk-based human verification. Operational examples include contract self-service, recurring employment drafting, document ingestion, contract intake and work routing, but reported gains are generally vendor- or company-reported and lack disclosed independent validation.

The common reasoning is that off-the-shelf generation is insufficient because legal work depends on connected processes, source access, organisational systems, client-specific risk tolerances and judgment accumulated through practice. Several sources add that this expertise can be difficult even for experienced lawyers to articulate, making its transfer into agents a continuing constraint rather than a solved engineering task. Human checkpoints are therefore usually treated as integral to accountability, although some sources warn that repeated verification can erase efficiency gains.

Material variation concerns the route to specialisation and the expected degree of autonomy. Some favour task-specific fine-tuning or lawyer-tagged data; others emphasise orchestration, retrieval, multiple models or purpose-built content without fine-tuning. Some describe narrow deployed agents and augmentation-oriented workflows, whereas broader end-to-end capabilities remain predictions. A few sources focus only on model improvements or general research benefits, leaving their position on the full proposition unclear. No supplied source clearly opposes the proposition, but this curated set should not be treated as representative of legal professionals, vendors or buyers generally.

qs.q: And so what we do is we actually hire domain experts who sit down and say, “These are the steps that I would take,” right?
qs.a: How AI Breakout Harvey is Transforming Legal Services, with CEO Winston Weinberg · Market & press · 2025

qs.q: When John and I first started working together, I mean, he would literally for hours on end sit over stand over my shoulder and just watch review contracts and just I mean, it drove me crazy because I realized I couldn't explain a lot of the things I was doing.
qs.a: Ryan Daniels — Crosby (AI-native law firm) · AI-native providers · 2025

elens.an:
The curated 2026 sources collectively accept the synthesis’s principal proposition and materially develop it with concrete operating models, architectures and evaluation methods. Across law firms, legal-AI vendors, AI-native providers and in-house examples, practical value is generally located not in raw text generation but in task-specific workflows that combine models with legal process design, specialised tools, authoritative sources, persistent matter or client context, and expert review. The material describes orchestration layers, firm-specific harnesses, client overlays, lawyer–legal-engineer–software-engineer collaboration, case-aware agents, risk-tiered approvals, and realistic synthetic matters with expert rubrics. It therefore moves the proposition from a general principle toward implementable designs.

The common reasons are that legal process knowledge is often absent from public training data; client preferences and matter history materially affect the answer; complex legal work can admit multiple defensible judgments; and model errors may be persuasive, unfamiliar or difficult to detect. These features make context engineering, evaluation and human accountability central. They also explain why current deployments are often narrower—intake, routing, information gathering, first-pass review, document extraction or supervised drafting—than the more ambitious claims about autonomous end-to-end work.

Material internal variation concerns degree, technical route and evidentiary confidence rather than the proposition’s core. Some sources predict complex end-to-end execution with oversight during 2026, while others regard fully autonomous in-house workflows as distant or potentially unattainable. Some favour highly specialised products, fine-tuning or firm-specific systems; others argue that general-purpose models already perform many simple transactional tasks adequately. Sources also vary between confidence that partner knowledge can be encoded through workflows, decision traces and client overlays, and emphasis on tacit judgment, subjective legal quality and weak feedback loops as barriers to transfer. Human review is widely retained, but several sources stress that verification can shift work to expensive senior lawyers and erode productivity gains. Reported operational improvements, adoption observations and benchmark-building practices are mostly company accounts, anecdotes, forecasts or methods without disclosed comparative results; they support implementation possibilities but do not establish broad legal reliability or workforce substitution.
